title: Harbor 2025 Law Department Survey Reveals Surge in AI Integration, Falling Outside Counsel Spend
author: Harbor · CLOC

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The survey materially extends the cluster with buyer-side evidence from large corporate legal departments: AI is being deployed in selected workflows alongside formal oversight, workflow technology, outside-counsel optimization and insourcing. This reinforces the claim that value depends on governed operating-model redesign, though the survey does not directly test general legal competence, verification quality or realised productivity.
qs: “Departments are shifting from reactive cost-containment to structured operational strategies – optimizing outside counsel, implementing workflow technologies, and building robust AI governance.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: Harbor directly supports the proposition that corporate legal departments are becoming the principal locus of AI adoption and buyer-side transformation. Its survey evidence links broad AI deployment and governance capacity with deliberate insourcing, tighter provider management, alternative fees, spending scrutiny and relatively stable staffing. It supports changing buyer behaviour and intentions more strongly than realised productivity gains or completed spending reductions.

st.t: Legal departments: AI supports selective sourcing redesign
st.an: Harbor/CLOC directly supports the cluster’s framing of AI as one component of broader legal-department operating-model redesign. Its evidence links AI governance and workflow technology with selective provider management and insourcing, while its spending figures concern expectations rather than proving uniform contraction or realized business value.

kp.d: Harbor's December 8, 2025 release reports findings from its 22nd annual corporate law department survey, conducted in collaboration with CLOC. The sample covers 135 departments across more than 15 industries, representing organizations with median revenue of $13 billion.
qs: Harbor today released benchmarking data from its 22nd annual survey of corporate law departments, in collaboration with CLOC (Corporate Legal Operations Consortium).
The survey captures insights from 135 corporate law departments across more than 15 industries, representing organizations with a median revenue of $13 billion.

kp.k: AI governance and deployment extend beyond exploration
kp.d: The survey reports that 85% of departments have a dedicated resource or committee managing AI. A majority have implemented or piloted tools for productivity, summarization, legal research, content creation and contract intelligence; the finding groups pilots and implementations together. Compliance, privacy, legal analysis and chatbots remain areas of active exploration.
qs: AI saw the most decisive shift of any category in the survey – 85% of departments now have a dedicated resource or committee managing AI efforts.
The majority have already implemented or piloted tools for productivity, summarization, legal research, content creation, and contract intelligence.
Departments are actively exploring emerging use cases in compliance, privacy, legal analysis, and chatbots.

kp.k: Harbor interprets AI adoption as enterprise integration
kp.d: Harbor's Jaime Woltjen characterizes adoption as a shift from experimentation to enterprise-level integration, with legal leaders deploying AI to improve productivity, research and content and contract workflows while building governance for responsible, secure use. These are Woltjen's interpretations of the adoption trend rather than quantified findings about productivity gains.
qs: Legal leaders are no longer simply exploring AI – they're deploying it to unlock productivity, accelerate legal research, and enhance content and contract workflows.
At the same time, departments are thoughtfully building governance frameworks to ensure responsible and secure use.
What we’re seeing is a shift from experimentation to enterprise-level integration.

kp.k: Fewer departments expect spending increases despite workload pressures
kp.d: Reported workload pressures persist in regulatory work (63%), cybersecurity/IT governance (58%) and contracts (53%). The share anticipating increased inside legal spending fell from 65% last year to 47%, while the share projecting outside counsel spending increases fell from 58% to 37%. These figures concern expectations of increases, rather than measured reductions in aggregate spending.
qs: As workload pressures persist, especially in regulatory (63%), cybersecurity/IT governance (58%), and contracts (53%), inside and outside counsel spend expectations dropped sharply year over year, signaling increased scrutiny and a push for efficiency.
Only 47% of departments anticipate increases in inside legal spending, down from 65% last year.
Outside counsel spend expectations saw a similar decline, from 58% projecting increases last year to 37% this year.

kp.k: Staffing forecasts stabilize and lawyer expansion expectations decline
kp.d: The release reports that 41% of departments expanded and 45% contracted in the past year, while most anticipated unchanged headcount in 2025. The share expecting lawyer headcount increases declined from 42% last year to 32%. The source presents this as staffing stabilization, without attributing the changes specifically to AI.
qs: While 41% of law departments expanded in the past year and 45% contracted, most anticipated headcount to remain unchanged in 2025.
Lawyer headcount predictions dropped noticeably: 32% of departments expect increases, down from 42% last year.

kp.k: Departments expand alternative fees, counsel panels and insourcing
kp.d: The survey reports alternative fee arrangement use at 76%, versus 70% last year. Departments that completed or are implementing convergence/preferred provider panels reached 61%, up from 50%; 65% intentionally sought to keep work in-house over the last one to two years. These are reported outside counsel optimization practices, not demonstrated consequences of AI adoption.
qs: More legal departments are formally optimizing outside counsel relationships, with 76% stating they use alternative fee arrangements (vs. 70% last year).
Furthermore, 61% completed or are implementing convergence/preferred provider panels (up sharply from 50%) and 65% made intentional efforts to keep work in-house in the last one to two years.

kp.k: Legal operations prioritizes technology, finances and provider management
kp.d: Departments identify technology strategy (80%), financial management (72%) and outside counsel/vendor management (62%) as priorities for the year ahead. Harbor's Lauren Chung interprets the findings as a move from reactive cost containment toward structured operational strategies combining outside counsel optimization, workflow technology and AI governance.
qs: Legal ops teams continue to expand their influence, with departments identifying technology strategy (80%), financial management (72%), and outside counsel/vendor management (62%) as top priorities for the year ahead.
Departments are shifting from reactive cost-containment to structured operational strategies – optimizing outside counsel, implementing workflow technologies, and building robust AI governance.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Harbor reports that corporate legal departments are moving from AI exploration toward deployment and more structured oversight; Jaime Woltjen characterizes this as enterprise-level integration aimed at improving legal workflows.
pts.d: Harbor states that 85% of surveyed departments have a dedicated resource or committee managing AI, and that a majority have implemented or piloted tools for productivity, summarization, legal research, content creation, and contract intelligence. Compliance, privacy, legal analysis, and chatbots remain emerging areas of exploration. Woltjen, Harbor's Senior Director of Strategy + Transformation, says departments are deploying AI to unlock productivity, accelerate research, and enhance content and contract workflows while building governance for responsible and secure use. Lauren Chung, Harbor's survey editor and Practice Group Lead, places robust AI governance within a broader shift toward structured operational strategies. Although the release juxtaposes AI adoption with lower expectations of spending increases and staffing stabilization, it does not establish that AI caused those spending or staffing patterns.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is Harbor and CLOC's 2025 survey of 135 corporate law departments, supplemented by Harbor executives' interpretation; measured productivity gains are not provided.
pts.d: The release draws on Harbor's 22nd annual corporate law department survey, conducted in collaboration with CLOC, covering more than 15 industries and organizations with median revenue of $13 billion. It supplies a numerical measure of AI oversight and a qualitative majority statement combining pilots and implementations. It does not give separate adoption rates by use case, an earlier AI adoption percentage, or measured changes in research speed, output quality, productivity, or costs attributable to AI. The productivity and enterprise-integration claims are Woltjen's interpretation of the trend, rather than reported performance-test results. Spending figures concern the share expecting increases, not a demonstrated fall in aggregate outside counsel spending.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims describe a transition reported in the 2025 survey, released December 8, 2025, rather than a dated prediction of future AI performance or displacement.
pts.d: The release describes dedicated AI oversight as existing 'now' and tools as already implemented or piloted. Other use cases are still being explored, so the source does not claim universal production deployment across legal activities. Woltjen presents governance development as occurring alongside deployment to support responsible and secure use. The broader setting is persistent workload and economic pressure. No deadline for full integration, quantified future efficiency gain, or prediction of AI-driven job losses is supplied.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected group is corporate in-house legal departments, especially legal leaders and legal operations teams responsible for technology strategy, workflows, and AI governance.
pts.d: The survey's organizational profile centers on large corporate buyers of legal services rather than law firms or individual consumers. In-house teams are described as integrating AI into research, summarization, content, and contract work; dedicated resources or committees manage AI efforts. Legal operations teams are presented as increasingly influential in technology strategy and operational management. Outside counsel face parallel client initiatives involving alternative fees, preferred-provider panels, and retaining work in-house, but the release does not specifically attribute those initiatives to AI. It makes no concrete claim about AI's effects on access to justice, junior-lawyer employment, or the public.
